docs.title: django-formwork
docs.text:
django-formwork is an opinionated UI framework for Django, built on Django forms. Forms are the central building block of most Django apps (CRUD pages, admin, search filters, sign-ups, content editors), so formwork treats the form as the primary UI surface: define a Form or ModelForm and you get DaisyUI styling, widgets that go beyond Django's built-ins, and the htmx + Alpine wiring that makes them dynamic without bespoke per-page JS. Set FORM_RENDERER once, build the CSS with Tailwind as the installation guide shows, include the JS template tag, and {{ form }} produces the full DaisyUI markup. Django's admin is unaffected, since it renders widgets directly, never {{ form }} or as_field_group(). The package also ships its own admin, built on these forms.

The widgets are Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox, ComboBoxMultiple, TextInput, Textarea, PasswordInput, SearchInput, DateInput, DatePicker, DateRangePicker, DateTimeRangePicker, StepperNumberInput, SuffixNumberInput, CheckboxInput, ToggleInput, CheckboxSelectMultiple, CardRadioSelect, CardCheckboxSelectMultiple, ClearableFileInput, FileDropzoneInput, ImageDropzoneInput, OTPInput, InputMask, Range, Rating, DataList, ValidatedTextarea and Display. Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox and ComboBoxMultiple search on the server when the widget gets a search_queryset, and the validated textarea posts to a view you write.

{% formwork_js %} loads an ES module that imports formwork-core.js (the formwork-morph htmx extension, dirty-field tracking, native-validation disabling) and the Alpine.data component of each widget. {{ form.media }} loads the same files per form, and a JS bundler can import them. The installation guide describes the three paths.

docs.title: Admin
docs.text: django_formwork.admin is a Django admin built on formwork forms, django-filter, htmx and Jinja2. It keeps the options, hooks, URL names and permissions of django.contrib.admin, so most admin.py modules port by changing from django.contrib import admin to from django_formwork import admin. The admin is experimental; Admin covers the setup and every option.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Python 3.14+, Django 6.0 or 6.1, DaisyUI 5, Tailwind CSS 4. DaisyUI and Tailwind are not bundled.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install django-formwork

# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [..., "django.forms", "django_iconx", "django_formwork"]
FORM_RENDERER = "django_formwork.FormworkRenderer"

<!-- base.html -->
{% load formwork static %}
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'dist.css' %}">  <!-- your Tailwind build of formwork.css -->
  <script src="https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@4.0.1/dist/htmx.min.js"></script>
  <script src="https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@4.0.1/dist/ext/hx-alpine-compat.min.js"></script>
  {% formwork_js %}
  <script defer src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/alpinejs@3/dist/cdn.min.js"></script>
</head>

<form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form }}
  <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>
</form>

The installation guide explains each setting and the script order.

docs.title: Design constraints
docs.text:
Django forms render at three levels:

  • The form ({{ form }}) renders all fields with labels, errors and help text.
  • The field ({{ field.as_field_group }}) renders one field with its label, errors and help text.
  • The widget ({{ field }}) renders the bare <input>, <select> or <textarea>.

Django admin renders only at the widget level, so formwork follows five constraints:

  1. Overriding form or field level rendering is admin-safe.
  2. Formwork never overrides a built-in widget template: it would reach admin and third-party forms. Built-ins are styled by CSS only; formwork's own widgets are opt-in.
  3. CSS is independent: admin and frontend load separate stylesheets.
  4. CSS styles all form elements globally: standalone inputs get DaisyUI styling without needing {{ form }}.
  5. Most formwork rules sit in @layer components, so a Tailwind utility class or unlayered project CSS overrides them.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text: FormworkRenderer is a TemplatesSetting renderer. It renders {{ form }} with formwork/forms/div.html and each field group with formwork/forms/field.html, and it loads every template through the project's TEMPLATES. A full render and an htmx swap of the search results therefore resolve the same template, and a project overrides any formwork template from its own template directories. Formwork uses its own template paths: shadowing django/forms/div.html from inside an app would change every form in every project that installs formwork.

docs.title: Widget design rules
docs.text:
These rules keep each widget in one place and each fix in one file. Follow them for a new widget and for a change to an existing one.

# Rule Reason R1 A widget has one class, one template, and at most one Alpine component. Add no fourth place. Python builds the context, the template holds the markup, and the JS module holds the behaviour. R2 Check field.widget_type in no template except field.html. Add a branch there only when the widget cannot do the work. Django takes the field wrapper from Field.template_name or the renderer, never from the widget. So only the wrapper can branch (single checkbox, toggle). R3 A widget template has no <script>, not even a small one. Register the behaviour with Alpine.data(name, …) in an alpine:init listener, import the module in formwork.js, and list it in the widget's Media. The template only names it: x-data="formworkSelect". A template that needs document.currentScript, a window.load listener, or a global from another library has its behaviour in the wrong file. R4 Follow Django's hierarchy. Subclass for the data contract, share the template, and override only the block that differs. SelectMultiple is a thin subclass over the shared SearchableSelectMixin. A domain variant, such as a project's own country select, subclasses Select and changes only the choices. When only the look of an option differs, return a ChoiceLabel and add no widget. Django's own SelectMultiple is three lines over Select. R5 Declare a widget by class, never with a multiple=True kwarg. Meta.widgets and ModelMultipleChoiceField.widget name a class, so the class is the contract. R6 Factor out shared behaviour and markup. Do not copy it. A variant extends the base template and overrides one block. The shared dropdown mechanics live once in dropdownBase() in widgets/_helpers.js. Each fix then goes in one place. R7 An inline Alpine attribute is one call: onToggle(), onNav($event, 1), matches($el). Move the value into the module if it contains ;, const, new …, or a JS literal built from {{ }}. Put a repeated attribute block in one x-bind object on the shared base. Pass values through data-* attributes. '{{ v\|escapejs }}' inside an expression parses only if escapejs escaped every quote. Bad: x-show="!search \|\| '{{ option.label\|escapejs }}'.toLowerCase()…". Good: x-show="matches($el)" data-label="{{ option.label }}". R8 Use native HTML first, Alpine second, and a library last: <details>/<summary> for a dropdown, <input type=search> for a filter, <button> for an action. The browser gives keyboard support and accessibility. R9 Put the id on the focusable control. A hidden input that has the field id is a bug. <label for> must point to an element that the user can click. R10 Keep server concerns in Python. A template builds no URL and no query parameter. Option markup goes through the #option_list partial. htmx swaps and full renders then use one code path. R11 The look of a widget is in its template, not in the Python class. A caller's attrs={"class": …} is only for a one-off variant. Add a CSS component class only after the same variant appears on a third page, and restate every hover and focus state in it. DaisyUI state rules win over a plain component class. R12 Name a widget after the primitive. Use Django's name for a drop-in replacement. Add a prefix only when two widgets coexist for one primitive. Do not name the library, the look, or a behaviour that is automatic. See Widget names.

docs.title: Widget names
docs.text:
Name Reason Select, SelectMultiple Django's names. Search appears past search_threshold, so it is not part of the name. TextInput, PasswordInput, DateInput Drop-in replacements, so no prefix. StepperNumberInput, SuffixNumberInput Two number inputs coexist, so both have a prefix. CardRadioSelect, CardCheckboxSelectMultiple The form is a card. "Big" would be subjective. ToggleInput The semantic. "Pill" would name the skin. SearchInput, ComboBox input type=search and the ARIA term. CountrySelect A domain choice set, not a rendering variant. Formwork ships no domain widgets; a project builds one from Select. ~~CalendarDateInput~~ Rejected: names the calendar library. ~~ComponentCheckboxSelectMultiple~~ Rejected: "Component" says nothing.

The names shadow django.forms on purpose. Widget modules write forms.Select, and callers write from django_formwork import widgets and widgets.Select.

docs.title: Adding a widget
docs.text:
1. Subclass the closest Django widget and set template_name.
  2. Compute the context in get_context. Keep the classes and the copy in the template.
  3. If the widget needs behaviour, add one Alpine.data module.
  4. For a variant, extend the base template and override one block.
  5. For server search, build on SearchableSelectMixin, so the form registers the search and FormworkSearchView serves it. Write no URL and no view.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: This guide builds one ticket form up from a single field to a searchable, server-validated form that saves, takes attachments, and edits existing records without re-validating untouched fields. Each step adds one capability. The snippets show the code that a step adds and leave out most imports, the URL configuration and the base template. The Person model has a name and an email, PRIORITY_CHOICES holds (value, label) pairs, and steps 5 and 6 show parts of the Ticket model. See the installation guide for the one-time CSS and JavaScript setup.

docs.title: Step 1: the form is the center
docs.text:
You render a form the normal Django way, and the default widgets take their styling from your DaisyUI theme.

# forms.py
class TicketTitleForm(forms.Form):
    title = forms.CharField(max_length=200, help_text="A short summary of the ticket.")

<!-- template.html -->
<form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form }}
  <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Create</button>
</form>

A plain text field needs no JavaScript. The richer widgets and the htmx integration in the later steps do, so put the scripts from installation step 5 in the base template's <head> from the start: htmx, its alpine-compat extension, {% formwork_js %}, then Alpine.

docs.title: Step 2: richer widgets
docs.text:
Formwork widgets add styling and behaviour that the Django widgets lack, such as a dropdown with search. Here the assignee is a Select backed by a model, with an initials badge and the person's email shown for each option. The priority stays a plain ChoiceField; standard fields and Formwork widgets mix freely in one form.

# forms.py
from django.utils.html import format_html

from django_formwork import ChoiceLabel, FormworkForm, widgets


class PersonChoiceField(forms.ModelChoiceField):
    def label_from_instance(self, person):
        initials = "".join(part[0] for part in person.name.split()[:2]).upper()
        return ChoiceLabel(
            person.name,
            icon=format_html("<span class='badge badge-neutral badge-sm'>{}</span>", initials),
            description=person.email,
        )


def people(request):
    return Person.objects.all()


class TicketWidgetsForm(FormworkForm):
    title = forms.CharField(max_length=200)
    assignee = PersonChoiceField(
        queryset=Person.objects.all(),
        widget=widgets.Select(search_queryset=people, search_fields=["name", "email"], search_decorator=None),
        required=False,
    )
    priority = forms.ChoiceField(choices=PRIORITY_CHOICES)

The dropdown searches on the server. Wire the endpoint once:

# urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path("__formwork__/", include("django_formwork.urls")),
]

search_queryset returns the rows to search; the endpoint calls it with the request. search_decorator is required. Pass an auth decorator such as login_required to protect the endpoint, or None for a public one. The ChoiceLabel icon is safe HTML; keep its attributes single-quoted so they nest inside the widget's markup.

docs.title: Step 3: server-side validation, still MPA
docs.text:
The server validates the form, and the page stays a multi-page app: htmx posts the form, the server renders it again, and htmx morphs the whole form back into the page, so the widget and focus state stay as they were.

# forms.py
class TicketValidatedForm(TicketWidgetsForm):
    def clean_title(self):
        title = self.cleaned_data["title"]
        if Ticket.objects.filter(title__iexact=title).exists():
            raise forms.ValidationError("A ticket with this title already exists.")
        return title

<!-- cookbook/_ticket_form.html -->
<form id="ticket-form" method="post"
      hx-post="{% url 'ck-step3' %}"
      hx-target="#ticket-form"
      hx-swap="outerMorph"
      data-formwork-dirty>
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form }}
  <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary mt-4">Save</button>
</form>

The form tag lives in a partial that step3.html wraps in the full page; the later steps reuse it, with the posting URL passed in as a variable. The view returns only the partial for htmx requests:

# views.py
def cookbook_step3(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = TicketValidatedForm(request.POST)
        form.is_valid()  # render any errors; the happy path arrives in step 4
        if request.headers.get("HX-Request") == "true":
            return render(request, "cookbook/_ticket_form.html", {"form": form})
        return render(request, "cookbook/step3.html", {"form": form})
    return render(request, "cookbook/step3.html", {"form": TicketValidatedForm()})

{% formwork_js %} registers the formwork-morph htmx extension, so the error tooltip appears without a full page reload and in-progress input is preserved. The title has no help text, so its error shows in a tooltip; a field with help text shows it inline. No hx-ext attribute is needed. The non-htmx branch keeps the plain form post working when JavaScript is unavailable. data-formwork-dirty highlights fields you have changed since the page loaded; it becomes useful on the edit form in step 6.

So far the view re-renders the form whether validation passed or not. Creating the ticket is the next step.

docs.title: Step 4: save the ticket
docs.text:
Tie the form to the model with FormworkModelForm and the view gets a regular form.save() happy path. is_valid() now runs the model's validators as well. The assignee field and the clean_title rule move over from steps 2 and 3 unchanged.

# forms.py
from django_formwork import FormworkModelForm


class TicketCreateForm(FormworkModelForm):
    assignee = PersonChoiceField(
        queryset=Person.objects.all(),
        widget=widgets.Select(search_queryset=people, search_fields=["name", "email"], search_decorator=None),
        required=False,
    )

    class Meta:
        model = Ticket
        fields = ["title", "assignee", "priority"]

    def clean_title(self):
        title = self.cleaned_data["title"]
        if Ticket.objects.filter(title__iexact=title).exists():
            raise forms.ValidationError("A ticket with this title already exists.")
        return title

# views.py
def cookbook_step4(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = TicketCreateForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            ticket = form.save()
            url = reverse("ck-created", args=[ticket.pk])
            if request.headers.get("HX-Request") == "true":
                return HttpResponse(headers={"HX-Redirect": url})
            return redirect(url)
        if request.headers.get("HX-Request") == "true":
            return render(request, "cookbook/_ticket_form.html", {"form": form})
        return render(request, "cookbook/step4.html", {"form": form})
    return render(request, "cookbook/step4.html", {"form": TicketCreateForm()})

htmx submits the form with fetch, so a normal redirect response would be followed in the background and morphed into the form. The HX-Redirect header tells htmx to navigate the browser instead. The non-htmx branch is the usual post/redirect/get.

docs.title: Step 5: attachments
docs.text:
Tickets carry screenshots. Add an ImageField to the model and swap its widget for a drop zone: drag an image in and a thumbnail preview shows before the upload.

# models.py
class Ticket(FormworkModel):
    # title, assignee, priority, description ...
    screenshot = models.ImageField(upload_to="screenshots/", blank=True)

# forms.py
class TicketUploadForm(TicketCreateForm):
    class Meta(TicketCreateForm.Meta):
        fields = [*TicketCreateForm.Meta.fields, "screenshot"]
        widgets = {"screenshot": widgets.ImageDropzoneInput(max_size=5 * 1024 * 1024)}

Uploads change two things outside the form class. The form tag gains the multipart attributes, and the view passes request.FILES:

<form id="ticket-form" method="post"
      enctype="multipart/form-data"
      hx-encoding="multipart/form-data"
      hx-post="{% url 'ck-step5' %}"
      hx-target="#ticket-form"
      hx-swap="outerMorph"
      data-formwork-dirty>

# views.py
form = TicketUploadForm(request.POST, request.FILES)

htmx does not read the form's enctype. Without hx-encoding="multipart/form-data" it submits the fields urlencoded and the file never reaches the server. enctype covers the no-JavaScript fallback, so keep both. max_size rejects an oversized file in the browser only, so check the size on the server yourself. upload_to needs the usual MEDIA_ROOT and MEDIA_URL settings.

docs.title: Step 6: skip validation for unchanged fields
docs.text:
The steps so far create tickets. Editing an existing one runs into a different problem: re-running validation on fields the user did not touch can reject legacy data that is fine to leave alone. Take a ticket titled LEGACY, saved before this validator existed:

# models.py
def reject_legacy_title(value):
    if value == "LEGACY":
        raise ValidationError("Legacy titles are no longer allowed.")


class Ticket(FormworkModel):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200, validators=[reject_legacy_title])
    # assignee, priority, description, screenshot ...

Set validate_dirty_only on a FormworkModelForm whose model inherits FormworkModel; the model base brings the dirty-field tracking the form needs. The field list holds only what this page edits.

# forms.py
class TicketEditForm(FormworkModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Ticket
        fields = ["title", "priority", "description"]
        validate_dirty_only = True

The view binds the form to the existing instance and saves as usual:

# views.py
def cookbook_step6(request):
    ticket = Ticket.objects.order_by("pk").first()
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = TicketEditForm(request.POST, instance=ticket)
        if form.is_valid():
            form.save()
        if request.headers.get("HX-Request") == "true":
            return render(request, "cookbook/_ticket_form.html", {"form": form})
        return render(request, "cookbook/step6.html", {"form": form})
    return render(request, "cookbook/step6.html", {"form": TicketEditForm(instance=ticket)})

Editing only the description of the LEGACY ticket now validates and saves. Unchanged fields skip their field validators, clean_<field> methods, model-level validation, and unique and constraint checks; their stored values carry through untouched. On create, the model's full_clean() covers every field as usual. See the forms reference for the exact rules.

On this form, data-formwork-dirty from step 3 highlights the fields you changed, which is the set that the server validates. The two mechanisms are independent. The browser draws the highlight, and the server decides what to skip by comparing the posted data against the loaded instance, with or without the attribute.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Validation can run async. The form base classes accept async clean_<field> and clean methods; async views call await form.ais_valid() and await form.asave(). See async validation.
  • Search does not need search_fields. Without them, search_queryset reads request.GET["q"] itself and returns its rows best first, for example from full-text search. On PostgreSQL, search_ranked=True ranks the matches and forgives typos. See server-side search.
  • Several forms on one page can each autosave their own fields of one row. See section forms.
  • The full example is a small task manager that combines these patterns with SelectMultiple, DatePicker, and a multi-step wizard.

The Forms, Widgets, and Views references document the details.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Five steps: install the package, configure Django, install the icons, build the CSS, and load htmx and Alpine.js for the dynamic widgets.

docs.title: 1. Install the package
docs.text:
pip install django-formwork

Or with uv:

uv add django-formwork

docs.title: 2. Configure Django
docs.text:
Add django.forms, django_iconx (a dependency that manages the icon set) and django_formwork to your installed apps, set the form renderer, and make sure you have a project-level static directory:

# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "django.forms",
    "django_iconx",
    "django_formwork",
]

# Every form renders through the formwork templates
FORM_RENDERER = "django_formwork.FormworkRenderer"

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "APP_DIRS": True,
        ...
    },
]

STATICFILES_DIRS = [BASE_DIR / "static"]

FormworkRenderer is a TemplatesSetting renderer: it loads templates through TEMPLATES, so a project template with the same path overrides any formwork template. "django.forms" supplies Django's own widget templates, and the DjangoTemplates backend must find app templates (APP_DIRS=True or the app_directories loader). django_iconx must be in INSTALLED_APPS for the next step to work. STATICFILES_DIRS tells the icon install where to put the downloaded files and lets Django serve them.

On startup, formwork imports the forms module of every installed app, so a form with a server-side search registers it before the first request.

manage.py check reports two setup mistakes: django_formwork.E001 when a form declares a server-side search but the URLconf does not include django_formwork.urls, and django_formwork.E002 when "django.forms" is missing from INSTALLED_APPS.

docs.title: 3. Install the icons
docs.text:
Formwork's widgets use Lucide icons, fetched at setup time rather than bundled. Run:

python manage.py formwork install

The command downloads the Lucide SVGs through django-iconx into <first STATICFILES_DIRS entry>/icons/lucide/. Then it generates iconx/icons.css in your static directory, with one CSS class per icon that points at the served SVG.

A second run downloads and generates the files again in place. Both output directories (static/icons/ and static/iconx/) are generated artifacts: gitignore them and run formwork install in CI and on fresh checkouts, or commit them if you prefer vendoring.

docs.title: Command reference: formwork install
docs.text:
python manage.py formwork install [--output DIR]
  • --output DIR: directory to write the generated CSS into (the file lands at DIR/iconx/icons.css). By default the command resolves your project static directory: the first entry of STATICFILES_DIRS if set, otherwise BASE_DIR/static. Use --output when your CSS build inputs live elsewhere.

The icon SVGs always go into the first STATICFILES_DIRS entry, because django-iconx downloads them there, so --output moves only the generated CSS. Without STATICFILES_DIRS the command uses BASE_DIR/static and prints a warning; add that directory to STATICFILES_DIRS, or Django does not serve the icons. With neither setting, the command stops with an error.

docs.title: 4. Build the CSS
docs.text:
Formwork uses DaisyUI 5 for component styling and Tailwind CSS 4+ for the build step. Formwork ships formwork.css, the Tailwind source. It contains @apply directives, @import "tailwindcss" and the DaisyUI @plugin, so build it with the Tailwind CLI or the PostCSS plugin, and import neither Tailwind nor DaisyUI a second time next to it.

Install the build tools:

npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/cli daisyui@5

Create your Tailwind input (say app.css in your project root):

/* Formwork's Tailwind source (already includes Tailwind + the DaisyUI plugin). */
@import "path/to/site-packages/django_formwork/static/formwork/formwork.css";

/* The icon classes generated by `manage.py formwork install` (step 3).
   In a layer, so that size-* utilities override the 1em icon size. */
@import "./static/iconx/icons.css" layer(components);

/* Your own templates. */
@source "./templates/";

Tailwind 4 only emits utility classes it finds in scanned sources. formwork.css registers the package templates, widgets and scripts with @source itself, and it safelists the {select,input,textarea}-{color} and badge-{color} classes, so your entry point lists only your own sources. Add an @source or an @source inline(...) for a class name that your code builds at render time, such as f"badge-{status}".

To find the site-packages path for the import line:

python -c "import django_formwork; print(django_formwork.__path__[0])"

Then build:

npx @tailwindcss/cli -i app.css -o static/dist.css

And link the built file in your base template:

{% load static %}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'dist.css' %}">

The examples/full app in the repository is a working copy of exactly this setup.

docs.title: DaisyUI version
docs.text: Formwork requires DaisyUI 5. DaisyUI 4 and earlier use a different component API and do not work with formwork. The CI builds the CSS with the DaisyUI 5 release pinned in the repository's package-lock.json.

docs.title: 5. htmx and Alpine.js
docs.text:
The dynamic widgets (dropdowns, server-side search, password reveal, steppers, drop zones, validated textarea) need htmx 4, htmx's alpine-compat extension and Alpine.js 3. Load them yourself, in this order:

{% load formwork %}
<script src="https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@4.0.1/dist/htmx.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@4.0.1/dist/ext/hx-alpine-compat.min.js"></script>
{% formwork_js %}
<script defer src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/alpinejs@3/dist/cdn.min.js"></script>
  1. htmx comes first, because the formwork modules register htmx extensions.
  2. The alpine-compat extension comes after htmx. It is required: without it a morph strips what Alpine bindings (x-show, x-text, :class, :aria-selected) wrote into the DOM.
  3. {% formwork_js %} comes before Alpine. Module scripts and defer scripts run in document order, and each formwork module registers its component in an alpine:init listener, which must exist when Alpine starts.

htmx 4 sends the server-side search and validation requests, and its built-in outerMorph swap morphs a re-rendered form into the page. {% formwork_js %} loads formwork.js as an ES module, which imports formwork-core.js (the formwork-morph htmx extension, dirty-field tracking, and native-validation disabling) plus each widget's Alpine.data component.

docs.title: htmx extensions
docs.text:
htmx 4 runs every registered extension on the whole page. If you restrict them with an htmx.config.extensions whitelist, list alpine-compat and formwork-morph, plus formwork-sections on a page that loads section forms.

formwork-core.js adds open to htmx.config.morphIgnore, so a morph leaves an open dropdown or disclosure as the user left it. For the same reason a server response cannot open or close a <details> or a <dialog> by morph; change the open state in the browser.

docs.title: JS loading paths
docs.text:
The {% formwork_js %} bundle is one tag and loads the core and every widget component. Two other paths load the same files.

For per-form loading via Django's Media, use {{ form.media }} for the widget JS the form actually contains, and add {% formwork_core_js %} for the page-global core (morph, dirty-tracking, validation disabling). Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox, DatePicker, DateRangePicker, DateTimeRangePicker, StepperNumberInput, PasswordInput, SearchInput, FileDropzoneInput, ImageDropzoneInput, InputMask and ValidatedTextarea each declare a Media class that points at their Alpine component file. Place both tags where {% formwork_js %} would go, before Alpine.

For a JS bundler (vite, webpack or esbuild), import formwork.js by its file path in the installed package, under the directory that the command in step 4 prints: import "path/to/site-packages/django_formwork/static/formwork/formwork.js";. The bundler follows the relative imports and emits one bundle, so the page needs no formwork template tag. The bundle must run after htmx and before Alpine, like the tag.

ES modules are deduplicated by URL, so mixing tags is harmless. Combining {% formwork_js %} and {% formwork_core_js %} on the same page still executes the core only once.

{% formwork_sections_js %} loads sections.js for section forms. The bundle leaves it out. Load it after htmx; it does not need Alpine.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: Every string that formwork shows (placeholders, button labels, the "N selected" counts, error messages) goes through Django's translation machinery. Formwork ships no message catalog: run makemessages in your project to collect the strings and translate them there. The JavaScript reads its translated texts from data-* attributes that the templates render, so the pages need no JavaScript catalog either.

docs.title: Basic form
docs.text:
With FORM_RENDERER set, any Django form renders with DaisyUI styling:

# forms.py
from django import forms


class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField()
    email = forms.EmailField()
    message = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea)

<!-- template.html; the base template loads the CSS and the scripts -->
<form method="post" class="max-w-md mx-auto">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form }}
  <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary mt-4">Send</button>
</form>

The installation guide shows the <head> with the scripts in the order they must load.

Each field renders inside a <fieldset class="fieldset"> with a label, help text and errors. A required field shows a red * after its label. Errors sit inline under a field that has help text and in a tooltip on a field without.

docs.title: Per-form styling
docs.text:
If you don't want to set FORM_RENDERER globally, use the form base classes:

# forms.py
from django import forms

from django_formwork import FormworkForm, FormworkModelForm

from .models import Profile


class ContactForm(FormworkForm):
    name = forms.CharField()
    email = forms.EmailField()


class ProfileForm(FormworkModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Profile
        fields = ["name", "bio", "avatar"]

docs.title: Formwork widgets
docs.text:
The widget names follow Django's and shadow django.forms on purpose, so import the module and write widgets.Select:

from django import forms

from django_formwork import widgets


class ExampleForm(forms.Form):
    # Toggle switch, with the label beside it
    dark_mode = forms.BooleanField(widget=widgets.ToggleInput, required=False)

    # Range slider
    volume = forms.IntegerField(widget=widgets.Range(attrs={"min": 0, "max": 100}))

    # Star rating
    rating = forms.TypedChoiceField(
        choices=widgets.Rating.make_choices(5),
        coerce=int,
        widget=widgets.Rating,
    )

    # Password with a show/hide button
    password = forms.CharField(widget=widgets.PasswordInput)

    # Dropdown; a search box appears past ten options
    country = forms.ChoiceField(
        choices=[("us", "United States"), ("de", "Germany")],
        widget=widgets.Select,
    )

    # Multi-select dropdown with checkboxes
    languages = forms.MultipleChoiceField(
        choices=[("py", "Python"), ("js", "JavaScript")],
        widget=widgets.SelectMultiple,
    )

    # Free text with suggestions
    topic = forms.CharField(
        widget=widgets.ComboBox(suggestions=["Python", "Django", "htmx"]),
    )

    # Number between - and + buttons
    seats = forms.IntegerField(widget=widgets.StepperNumberInput(integer=True, min=1))

    # Native date input
    start = forms.DateField(widget=widgets.DateInput)

    # Drag-and-drop file upload
    attachment = forms.FileField(widget=widgets.FileDropzoneInput)

    # Image upload with preview
    avatar = forms.ImageField(widget=widgets.ImageDropzoneInput)

The widget reference lists every widget and its parameters.

docs.title: Server-side textarea validation
docs.text:
ValidatedTextarea sends the textarea content to a server-side view as the user types, and highlights error spans in real time.

# views.py
import re

from django_formwork import FormworkValidateView

TYPOS = {"teh": "the", "recieve": "receive"}


class SpellCheckView(FormworkValidateView):
    def get_errors(self, text: str, **kwargs) -> list[dict]:
        return [
            {
                "message": f"Did you mean {TYPOS[word.group().lower()]!r}?",
                "start": word.start(),
                "end": word.end(),
            }
            for word in re.finditer(r"\w+", text)
            if word.group().lower() in TYPOS
        ]

# urls.py
from django.urls import path

from .views import SpellCheckView

urlpatterns = [
    path("validate/spell/", SpellCheckView.as_view(), name="spell-check"),
]

# forms.py
from django import forms
from django.urls import reverse_lazy

from django_formwork import widgets


class PostForm(forms.Form):
    content = forms.CharField(
        widget=widgets.ValidatedTextarea(validate_url=reverse_lazy("spell-check")),
    )

The textarea sends its text only when it has an id. A form field gets one from the form's auto_id. A form with auto_id=False, or a widget rendered without attrs={"id": ...}, renders a textarea that never validates.

CSRF exemption

FormworkValidateView is CSRF-exempt because it only reads the posted text. Use it for read-only checks. A view that writes to the database or sends an email needs a regular Django view with CSRF protection.

docs.title: Server-side search
docs.text:
Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox and ComboBoxMultiple search on the server when the widget gets a search_queryset. Wire the URL pattern once:

# urls.py
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path("__formwork__/", include("django_formwork.urls")),
]

Then give the widget the rows to search, the fields to match and an access rule:

# forms.py
from django import forms
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required

from django_formwork import FormworkForm, widgets

from .models import City


def cities(request):
    return City.objects.filter(active=True)


class CityForm(FormworkForm):
    city = forms.ModelChoiceField(
        queryset=City.objects.filter(active=True),
        widget=widgets.Select(
            search_queryset=cities,
            search_fields=["name", "country__name"],
            search_decorator=login_required,
        ),
    )

The form class registers the search when Python creates it. Formwork imports the forms module of each installed app at startup, so a search declared there works in every worker from the first request. search_queryset is a callable that takes the request; the endpoint calls it for each search, so it can scope the rows to the user. search_decorator is required: pass an auth decorator such as login_required, or None for a public endpoint. The views reference covers the endpoint, paging, ranked search and search templates.

docs.title: Template tags
docs.text:
{% load formwork %}

<!-- JS module: core plus every widget component; load it after htmx and before Alpine -->
{% formwork_js %}

<!-- Section forms (opt-in); load it after htmx -->
{% formwork_sections_js %}

<!-- Hidden input that names the section a section form saves -->
{% formwork_section "general" %}

docs.title: Admin
docs.text:
django_formwork.admin is a Django admin built on formwork forms, django-filter, htmx and Jinja2, styled with DaisyUI. It keeps the names, options, hooks, URL names and permissions of django.contrib.admin, so most admin.py modules port by changing one import:

# from django.contrib import admin
from django_formwork import admin


@admin.register(Ticket)
class TicketAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ["subject", "requester", "status", "priority"]
    list_filter = ["status", "opened_at"]
    search_fields = ["subject", "requester__email"]
    inlines = [ReplyInline]

The classes are its own. A ModelAdmin does not subclass Django's, so an admin class written for django.contrib.admin that calls into Django's internals needs changes.

Experimental

The admin is new and its API can change in any release before 1.0.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install "django-formwork[admin]"

The admin extra installs django-filter and Jinja2.

docs.title: 2. Settings
docs.text:
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django.contrib.admin",  # the history log (LogEntry)
    "django.contrib.auth",
    "django.contrib.contenttypes",
    "django.contrib.messages",
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "django.forms",
    "django_iconx",
    "django_formwork",
    "django_formwork.admin",
]

MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
    ...,
]

The admin writes its history to Django's LogEntry, so django.contrib.admin must be installed. Its system checks also ask for a DjangoTemplates backend with the request, auth and messages context processors. The admin pages themselves render through a private Jinja2 engine, so TEMPLATES needs no Jinja2 backend.

Run manage.py migrate after you add the app.

manage.py check reports a missing app or middleware, and checks every registered ModelAdmin for the mistakes Django's admin checks catch, under the same numbers: formwork_admin.E108 for an unknown list_display entry, formwork_admin.E116 for a broken list_filter entry, and so on.

docs.title: 3. URLs
docs.text:
from django.urls import include, path

from django_formwork.admin import site

urlpatterns = [
    path("__formwork__/", include("django_formwork.urls")),
    path("admin/", site.urls),
]

django_formwork.urls serves the relation search of the dropdowns. The site's URL names match Django's, so reverse("admin:helpdesk_ticket_change", args=[ticket.pk]) works as before. To run Django's admin next to this one, give one of the two sites another name, since both use the admin namespace by default.

docs.title: 4. CSS
docs.text:
Import admin.css after formwork.css in your Tailwind entry and build it as in Installation:

@import "path/to/site-packages/django_formwork/static/formwork/formwork.css";
@import "path/to/site-packages/django_formwork/admin/static/formwork_admin/admin.css";
@import "./static/iconx/icons.css" layer(components);

admin.css registers the admin's templates with @source, so Tailwind finds their classes. Then point the site at the built file:

# myproject/admin_site.py
from django_formwork.admin import AdminSite


class MyAdminSite(AdminSite):
    site_header = "Helpdesk"
    stylesheets = ("dist.css",)

# settings.py
FORMWORK_ADMIN_SITE = "myproject.admin_site.MyAdminSite"

The navigation and the actions use Lucide icons, so run manage.py formwork install once, as for the widgets.

docs.title: 5. Scripts
docs.text: The site loads htmx 4, its Alpine bridge and Alpine.js from a CDN. To serve them yourself, override scripts (htmx and the bridge) and alpine_script on your site class.

docs.title: The site
docs.text:
django_formwork.admin.site is the default site. FORMWORK_ADMIN_SITE names its class, and every app's admin module is imported at startup (FORMWORK_ADMIN_AUTODISCOVER changes the module name). Attributes of AdminSite that Django's site does not have:

Attribute Default Description stylesheets ("formwork/formwork-dist.css",) Static paths of the built CSS. scripts htmx 4 and hx-alpine-compat Scripts loaded before the admin's own. alpine_script Alpine.js 3.15 Loaded last, with defer. themes ("light", "dark") The DaisyUI themes the theme menu offers. The first is the default.

site_title, site_header, index_title, site_url, empty_value_display, enable_nav_sidebar, login_form, password_change_form, the *_template attributes, each_context(), get_app_list(), admin_view(), has_permission(), add_action() and disable_action() work as in Django.

docs.title: ModelAdmin
docs.text:
The list, add, change, delete and history pages read the same options as Django's admin: list_display, list_display_links, list_filter, list_select_related, list_per_page, list_max_show_all, list_editable, search_fields, search_help_text, date_hierarchy, ordering, sortable_by, fields, exclude, fieldsets, readonly_fields, prepopulated_fields, radio_fields, autocomplete_fields, raw_id_fields, formfield_overrides, form, inlines, actions, save_as, save_on_top, preserve_filters, view_on_site, the has_*_permission() methods, and the get_*(), save_model(), save_formset(), delete_model() and response_*() hooks.

The forms are formwork forms, so every field renders with formwork's widgets and templates. A relation gets a Select or SelectMultiple, a date field a DatePicker, and a datetime field a DatePicker with a time input next to it. As in Django's admin, a date is typed in the first format of the language's DATE_INPUT_FORMATS, for example 10.01.2026 in German, and the date filter writes its dates the same way. Lists and read-only fields show DATE_FORMAT and DATETIME_FORMAT.

After a failed save, each field error shows under its field, as in Django's admin. A form whose Meta.error_display is set keeps that display.

Options this admin adds:

Option Description icon The Lucide icon next to the model in the navigation and the page title. Unset, the model gets a placeholder shape, see below. list_badges Badge colors per value, by column: {"status": {"active": "success", "archived": "warning"}}. list_only_fields Load only these columns on the list page. list_defer_fields Skip these columns on the list page, for a large JSON or text column that no column shows.

list_only_fields is opt-in. A __str__ that reads a deferred field runs one query per row.

A model without an icon gets a plain shape instead: a circle, triangle, square, diamond, pentagon, hexagon or star. The shape comes from a hash of the model's label, so it stays the same across restarts, and the models of one app get different shapes while there are no more than seven of them. Set icon on the models you want to tell apart at a glance and leave the rest to the shapes.

docs.title: Related objects
docs.text:
Next to a relation, the change form has buttons that open the related model's admin in a dialog. Django's admin opens a popup window for the same buttons. They show next to any widget of the relation: the dropdown, the radio buttons of radio_fields, or a widget from formfield_overrides, such as checkboxes or a native select. A hidden widget gets no buttons, as in Django's admin.

  • Add another (plus) adds a row. After the save, the dialog closes and the field chooses the new row. Every other field that can choose the row lists it too, also in inline rows added later.
  • Change selected (pencil) edits the chosen row, and the field shows its new name. With only the view permission, the button is an eye and shows the row. Without a chosen row, the button stays in place, dimmed. A many-to-many field has no such button.

Each button shows only with the matching permission on the related model's admin. There is no delete button: delete a row in its own admin.

A relation in the dialog opens the next dialog on top. Esc or the close button closes a dialog, and the browser asks first when its form has unsaved changes. A click with Ctrl or Cmd, or with the middle button, opens the page in a new tab instead.

The dialog loads Django's popup URLs, with _popup=1 and _to_field, so a response_add(), response_change() or response_delete() that checks for _popup keeps working. A save in the dialog ends on popup_response_template, by default formwork_admin/popup_response.html. An override keeps the element with the id formwork-admin-popup-response: the dialog reads the saved row from its data-popup-response attribute.

After a save in the dialog, the change form posts its values to its own URL with _refresh added, and htmx morphs the page with the response. For such a POST, changeform_view() renders the form as posted and saves nothing. Field errors show only when the page showed them before. An override of changeform_view() that acts on a POST checks for _refresh first.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
The filter bar is a django-filter FilterSet that the admin builds from list_filter. An entry can be:

  • a field name. Choices, booleans and relations get a dropdown, dates a range picker. Its calendar has the ranges of Django's date filter: Today, Past 7 days, This month and This year.
  • a SimpleListFilter subclass, as in Django.
  • a tuple such as ("field", admin.EmptyFieldListFilter) or ("category", admin.RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter).
  • a django_filters.Filter with its field_name set, for any lookup django-filter supports. A django_filters.RangeFilter shows a min and a max input in one field.

The filters sit in a row under the search box, in the order of list_filter. The Filters button opens the row and shows how many filters are active. The row is open when the page loads with an active filter. A list without list_filter keeps the button in the same place, and its row says that the list has no filters.

The search box filters the same way, through get_search_results(), so ^, = and @ prefixes in search_fields work as in Django. A filter on a many-to-many relation picks one row, as Django's related filter does.

The list updates as the user types or picks, and the URL keeps every filter, the search, the sort and the page.

With show_facets at its default, admin.ShowFacets.ALLOW, the filter row has a Show counts switch. The switch adds _facets to the URL, as Django's link does, and each option then shows how many rows it matches. The count applies the search and the other filters, but not the filter of the option itself. ShowFacets.ALWAYS shows the counts without the switch, and ShowFacets.NEVER removes both.

@admin.register(Project)
class ProjectAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_filter = ("status", "owner")
    show_facets = admin.ShowFacets.ALWAYS

Each filter with counts runs one more query. Date and number ranges have no counts. A relation filter that searches its rows on the server shows counts only while all rows fit on its first page of 20.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
When the columns of list_display do not fit the width of the list, the list hides columns from the right and shows a "+N" button at the end of the header. The checkbox, the first column and the columns of list_display_links always show. The tooltip of the button names the hidden columns.

The button shows all columns. The table then scrolls sideways, and the checkbox and the first column stay in view. The browser stores the choice per model, so the list opens the same way next time.

A list_editable error in a hidden column shows all columns and scrolls the first error into view. Without JavaScript, the table scrolls sideways as in Django's admin.

docs.title: Info dialog
docs.text:
The info button next to the list's title opens a dialog about the model:

  • the row count, from the same paginator as the list, so a large PostgreSQL table shows its estimate.
  • every entry of search_fields with its label and how a word matches: contains, starts with, is or full text. search_help_text shows above them.
  • every field with its type, the related model and flags such as unique, indexed or null, and the list's default order.

A superuser also sees the table: its name, the database and its version, the model and admin classes, the indexes and constraints the database has, and the size of the rows and the indexes on PostgreSQL, MySQL and on SQLite builds with the dbstat table. The dialog loads from the info/ URL the first time it opens, so the list page runs no extra queries. Override formwork_admin/change_list_info.html to change what it shows.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
@admin.action takes two more arguments:

@admin.action(description="Archive selected tickets", icon="archive", danger=True)
def archive(self, request, queryset): ...

icon names a Lucide icon for the action bar, and danger draws the button in the error color. Actions run as in Django: a function gets (modeladmin, request, queryset) and a name resolves to a method of the admin. The bar appears when a row is selected, and shift-click selects a range.

docs.title: Inlines
docs.text: TabularInline and StackedInline take Django's options (extra, min_num, max_num, fk_name, can_delete, show_change_link, classes, formset). Rows are added and removed in the browser, and the formset indexes stay contiguous.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
The Export menu next to the add button writes the list as a CSV, Excel or JSON file. The file holds every row that the filters and the search let through, in the list's sort order, not only the current page.

@admin.register(Ticket)
class TicketAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    export_fields = ["id", "subject", "requester__email", "status", "opened_at", "age"]
    export_formats = ("csv", "xlsx")
Option Default Description export_fields every field The columns: field names, __ lookups, admin methods and callables, as in list_display. export_formats ("csv", "xlsx", "json") The formats the menu offers. An empty tuple hides the menu. export_background_threshold 5000 Above this many rows the export runs as a task. None keeps every export in the request.

A foreign key exports the primary key of the related row, a many-to-many field the sorted primary keys. Excel keeps numbers, dates and booleans as such. JSON writes dates and decimals as text, as DjangoJSONEncoder does. A JSON field stays structured in JSON and becomes JSON text in CSV and Excel. Excel shows a datetime in the site's time zone, since Excel has no time zones. The CSV file starts with a byte order mark, so Excel reads it as UTF-8.

Excel files need openpyxl. Without it, the menu leaves Excel out.

Whoever can see the list can export it. has_export_permission() changes that, and get_export_fields(), get_export_queryset() and get_export_formats() take the request like the other get_*() hooks. A new format subclasses formats.FileFormat, implements write() and read(), and goes into formats.FORMATS under its name.

docs.title: Large exports
docs.text:
Above export_background_threshold, the admin saves an ExportJob and queues it on Django's task framework after the request's transaction commits. The list then shows a message with a link to the Exports page. That page is in the account menu. It lists the user's last 50 exports and refreshes while one still runs. The file goes to the default storage under formwork_admin/exports/, and only the user who started the export can download it.

The job runs as that user with the list's filters, search and sort, so a get_queryset() that limits the rows per user limits the file too.

Django's default task backend, ImmediateBackend, runs the job inside the request, so the file is ready when the list loads again. For a real background run, set TASKS to a backend with a worker. To use another queue, override enqueue_export() on your site:

from celery import shared_task

from django_formwork.admin import AdminSite
from django_formwork.admin.exports import run_export_job


@shared_task
def run_admin_export(job_id):
    run_export_job(job_id)


class MyAdminSite(AdminSite):
    def enqueue_export(self, job):
        run_admin_export.delay(job.pk)

The admin does not delete old exports. ExportJob.delete() deletes the row and its file.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
Import is off by default. import_formats turns it on and adds an Import button next to the Export menu:

@admin.register(Contact)
class ContactAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    import_formats = ("csv", "xlsx")
    import_id_fields = ["email"]
Option Default Description import_formats () The formats the Import page reads. An empty tuple hides the button. import_fields the add form's fields The fields a row sets. Unset, the fields of the add form without the read-only and file fields. import_id_fields the primary key The fields that find the record a row changes.

The import page checks a file before it saves anything. Pick a file and click Check file. The preview counts the new, changed, unchanged and invalid rows, and a click on a count shows only those rows. A changed cell shows the old and the new value, and an invalid cell shows its error as in list_editable. Import saves the rows in one transaction and goes back to the list with a summary. While a row has an error, the Import button stays off: fix the file and check it again.

How the file maps to records:

  • A header matches a field by its name or its label, in any case. Other columns are listed as ignored, so a file exported from the list imports as it is.
  • A row whose import_id_fields match a record changes that record. A row without a match, or with an empty key, adds a new one. Two rows for the same record are an error.
  • A foreign key column holds the primary key, as the export writes it. A header such as category__name finds the record by that field instead. A many-to-many column holds the keys separated by commas, and tags__slug works the same way. A value that matches no record or several records is an error.
  • A choice column takes the stored value or the label. A boolean column takes true and false or yes and no.
  • A column the file leaves out keeps the record's value on a changed row and gets the field's default on a new row. Records the file does not mention stay as they are. An import never deletes.
  • A row that matches its record is skipped: it is not saved and not logged.

Each row runs through the admin's form in a formwork model formset, so the form's validation applies. Unique fields are checked across the whole file: two rows with the same email get the error Django would give, with one query per check instead of one per row. Saving goes through save_form(), save_model() and save_related(), so an override that sets an owner still runs. Each saved row gets a history entry with Django's change message.

The formats:

  • CSV in UTF-8, with or without a byte order mark, or in Windows-1252. The delimiter is a comma, a semicolon or a tab, whichever the header row has most of. In a file with semicolons, a number can use a decimal comma, as a German Excel saves it.
  • Excel reads the first sheet. It needs openpyxl.
  • JSON reads a list of objects.

Whoever can add or change records can import. Each row is checked again: a new row needs has_add_permission(), a changed row has_change_permission() on its record. A row that fails gets an error. has_import_permission(), get_import_formats(), get_import_fields(), get_import_id_fields() and get_import_form() take the request like the other hooks.

The import keeps no copy of the file between the check and the import. Import sends the file again, and the server checks it again. If the file or the records changed since the check, the page shows the new preview instead of importing. The import runs in the request, so a very large file is better split. The preview shows up to 1,000 rows: the ones with errors first, then the changed and the new ones. The counts cover every row.

docs.title: Users and groups
docs.text:
With django.contrib.auth installed, the site registers admins for User and Group, as django.contrib.auth.admin does on Django's own site. They work as Django's do:

  • Add user asks for a username and a password, or turns password-based authentication off. The save opens the change form of the new user for the other fields.
  • The change form shows the algorithm and the parameters of the password hash. Its button opens a page that sets a new password or turns password-based authentication off.
  • To add a user, the "Change user" permission is necessary too, because a user who can add users can add a superuser.
  • The permissions of a group or a user are grouped by model.

When AUTH_USER_MODEL names another model, only Group is registered. For a model that extends AbstractUser, subclass UserAdmin:

from django_formwork import admin
from django_formwork.admin.auth import UserAdmin

from .models import Account


@admin.register(Account)
class AccountAdmin(UserAdmin):
    list_display = ("username", "email", "is_staff")

User and Group are registered before the admin modules of the apps are imported, so an app can replace them:

from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, User

from django_formwork import admin
from django_formwork.admin.auth import UserAdmin

admin.site.unregister(Group)
admin.site.unregister(User)


@admin.register(User)
class StaffUserAdmin(UserAdmin):
    list_filter = ("is_active",)

django_formwork.admin.auth also has UserChangeForm, AdminUserCreationForm and AdminPasswordChangeForm for form, add_form and change_password_form, and GroupAdmin. change_user_password_template names the template of the password page.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Every page is a Jinja2 template under formwork_admin/, loaded from the jinja2/ directory of each installed app. To override one, put a template with the same path in an app listed before django_formwork.admin:

myapp/jinja2/formwork_admin/change_list.html

change_list_template, change_form_template and the other *_template options name Jinja2 templates of the same engine.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• A foreign key column joins only its own relation. Django's admin calls select_related() without arguments for one, which follows every non-null relation five levels deep.
  • A relation to a model whose admin has search_fields pages its rows from the server. The change form no longer loads the whole related table into a <select>.
  • Without filters, the list counts a PostgreSQL table of more than 10,000 rows from the planner's estimate instead of COUNT(*). Any filter or search counts exactly. EstimatedCountPaginator.estimate_threshold sets the limit.
  • A search or filter that can return a row twice keeps the rows unique with a primary key subquery instead of DISTINCT over every column.
  • The filter bar, the search and the paging swap only the list, without a full page load.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text: Keys Action Ctrl+K Filter the navigation / Focus the list search Ctrl+S Save and continue editing
