docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
FormworkForm and FormworkModelForm bundle the DaisyUI renderer with behaviours plain Django forms do not have: search registration, a choice of error placement, mandatory fields, dirty-only validation, and async validation and saving. section_forms() builds the forms of a page that saves one row in several sections.

With FORM_RENDERER = "django_formwork.FormworkRenderer" set, every form in the project renders styled, including plain forms.Form. Reach for the base classes when you want the behaviours below, or formwork styling on individual forms without the global renderer.

Everything documented here is importable from the package root:

from django_formwork import FormworkForm, FormworkModel, FormworkModelForm, section_forms

docs.title: Base classes
Search registration
docs.text: A field whose widget (Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox or ComboBoxMultiple) has a search_queryset registers its search when Python creates the form class. Formwork imports the forms module of every installed app at startup, so the search exists in every worker before the first request. A single include("django_formwork.urls") serves all of them. Registration raises ImproperlyConfigured for a widget without search_decorator: pass an auth decorator such as login_required, or None for a public endpoint. A bad Meta option fails the same way, when Python creates the class: an error_display other than "auto", "inline" or "tooltip", a mandatory that is a string or names a field the form lacks, and validate_dirty_only on a model without get_dirty_fields(). See Views for the endpoint and the quickstart for a worked example.

docs.title: Required and mandatory fields
docs.text:
A required field shows a red * after its label, and the widget carries aria-required="true". A disabled field shows no asterisk. Formwork marks no optional field.

Meta.mandatory names fields that a save accepts empty but a later step needs, for example a draft that the user publishes later. They get the asterisk and aria-required too, and they still validate as optional:

class ListingForm(FormworkModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Listing
        fields = ["title", "price", "description"]
        mandatory = ["price", "description"]

Meta.mandatory seeds the set self.mandatory. Add a name that depends on the data after super().__init__():

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if self.instance.category == "vehicle":
            self.mandatory.add("mileage")

docs.title: Help text
docs.text:
Formwork escapes help text. Django's own templates render it as HTML, so a plain string with tags that showed as markup there shows the tags as text here. Build markup with format_html() or mark_safe():

from django.utils.html import format_html

email = forms.EmailField(
    help_text=format_html('See the <a href="{}">privacy policy</a>.', "/privacy/"),
)

docs.title: error_display
docs.text:
error_display picks where field errors render:

Value Placement "auto" (default) inline when the field has help text, in a tooltip when it has none "inline" inline under every field "tooltip" in a DaisyUI tooltip on every field

Set it on the Meta class or per instantiation:

class ContactForm(FormworkForm):
    class Meta:
        error_display = "tooltip"


# or
form = ContactForm(request.POST, error_display="tooltip")

An inline error uses the pattern of the help text: a small icon below the widget, in error color, with the message truncated to one line and a [more] toggle when it overflows. [more] reveals the full error and the help text together; [less] collapses both. While collapsed, the help text is present for screen readers but visually hidden. A tooltip error is more compact, but a user can miss it in a dense layout such as a table row.

Use "inline" for inline table-row editing, dense multi-column layouts, or forms where the help text must stay reachable while an error shows, and "tooltip" for fields with room around them. A plain forms.Form rendered by FormworkRenderer uses "auto".

docs.title: validate_dirty_only
docs.text:
On an edit form, validators added after a record was saved can reject stored values the user never touched. validate_dirty_only skips validation for fields the submission did not change. Enable it on the Meta class or per instantiation:

class TicketEditForm(FormworkModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Ticket
        fields = ["title", "priority", "description"]
        validate_dirty_only = True


# or
form = TicketEditForm(request.POST, instance=ticket, validate_dirty_only=True)

For a field the user did not change:

  • field validators and the clean_<field> method do not run
  • model field validation, unique checks, and constraint checks exclude it
  • the stored value is carried into cleaned_data and left untouched on the instance, so an unchanged relation is never re-assigned

A field that the post leaves out counts as unchanged, so a form that posts only its changed fields (a section form with data-send-changed) validates only those. Changed fields validate as usual, and the form-wide clean() method always runs. Form.changed_data decides whether a field counts as changed: it compares the posted value against the initial data of the form, and with instance= bound, the initial data is what the database holds. The model-level exclusions apply only to existing instances. On create, the full_clean() of the instance covers every field.

On a FormworkModelForm the flag requires the model to provide get_dirty_fields(). Inherit FormworkModel, or mix filthyfields.DirtyFieldsMixin into the model directly; the form raises ImproperlyConfigured otherwise. Plain FormworkForm supports the flag too, where it covers the field-level skips.

The cookbook walks through a legacy-data example.

docs.title: Async validation and saving
docs.text:
ais_valid(), afull_clean(), and asave() are async counterparts to Django's sync methods. clean_<field>() and clean() can be sync or async in the same form. Formwork detects the async ones and awaits them, so validation can use the async ORM without sync_to_async wrappers.

from django import forms
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError

from django_formwork import FormworkForm


class SignupForm(FormworkForm):
    email = forms.EmailField()

    async def clean_email(self):
        email = self.cleaned_data["email"]
        if await User.objects.filter(email__iexact=email).aexists():
            raise ValidationError("Already registered.")
        return email


async def signup(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = SignupForm(request.POST)
        if await form.ais_valid():
            ...

asave(commit=True) mirrors ModelForm.save(): it awaits the instance's asave() and then saves many-to-many relations. With commit=False it returns the unsaved instance and exposes asave_m2m as an async callable; call await form.asave_m2m() after saving the instance. Calling the sync save_m2m hook on a form saved with asave(commit=False) raises RuntimeError that points to asave_m2m().

Set FORMWORK_FORCE_ASYNC = True in settings to make the sync entry points (is_valid(), full_clean(), save()) raise RuntimeError. Use it to keep accidental sync calls out of an async codebase.

Without the setting, a form with an async clean_<field>() or clean() that validates through the sync is_valid() stores the un-awaited coroutine in cleaned_data and skips the check. Enable FORMWORK_FORCE_ASYNC in a project that defines async validators and touches forms from sync code, including a template that reads form.errors. The sync call then raises RuntimeError.

Formwork's model formsets validate their forms through the sync path, so their forms are exempt from the setting; see Formsets. FormworkRowSaveMixin calls the sync is_valid(), so a row save fails while the setting is on.

docs.title: Section forms
docs.text:
A section form saves its own fields of one row, without a submit button: it posts on every change and morphs itself back from the response. Several section forms on one page share a request queue, so their saves run in order.

section_forms(request, sections, **kwargs) builds every section's form and binds only the one that the POST names. The keyword arguments go to each form, for example instance=. A POST that names no known section raises BadRequest.

from django_formwork import section_forms


def edit_project(request, pk):
    project = get_object_or_404(Project, pk=pk)
    sections = section_forms(
        request,
        {"general": ProjectGeneralForm, "extras": ProjectExtrasForm},
        instance=project,
    )
    for form in sections.values():
        if form.is_bound and form.is_valid():
            form.save()
    return render(request, "project_edit.html", {"sections": sections})

{% load formwork %}
<div data-section-forms>
  <form id="general_form" data-section-form novalidate
        hx-post="{{ request.path }}" hx-trigger="change delay:300ms"
        hx-select="#general_form" hx-swap="outerMorph"
        hx-sync="closest [data-section-forms]:queue all">
    {% csrf_token %}{% formwork_section "general" %}
    {{ sections.general }}
  </form>
  <form id="extras_form" data-section-form data-send-changed novalidate
        hx-post="{{ request.path }}" hx-trigger="change delay:300ms"
        hx-select="#extras_form" hx-swap="outerMorph"
        hx-sync="closest [data-section-forms]:queue all">
    {% csrf_token %}{% formwork_section "extras" %}
    {{ sections.extras }}
  </form>
</div>

Load {% formwork_sections_js %} after htmx. The formwork bundle leaves it out, and it does not need Alpine.

  • {% formwork_section "name" %} writes the hidden _formwork_section input that names the section.
  • Every section form needs hx-sync="closest [data-section-forms]:queue all". A dropped or replaced save leaves its change unsent, and a request that waits for that save then never runs.
  • A response to a save that is older than the latest change leaves the form alone; the queued request after it carries that change.
  • A request that replaces section forms (a tab switch, for example) waits until their saves are answered. Leaving the page during a save asks for confirmation.
  • data-send-changed on a form posts only the fields that differ from the last valid render, plus csrfmiddlewaretoken and _formwork_section. With a value, data-send-changed="<prefix>" also posts every field whose name starts with <prefix>, changed or not. Pair it with validate_dirty_only, so the fields the post leaves out keep their stored values.
  • data-section-indicator="<selector>" on a field wrapper shows that indicator while a save the field started runs.

docs.title: FormworkModel
docs.text:
FormworkModel is an abstract model base that mixes in filthyfields.DirtyFieldsMixin, providing the get_dirty_fields() that validate_dirty_only needs, and adds one helper for clean() rules:

class Ticket(FormworkModel):
    status = models.CharField(max_length=10)
    closed_at = models.DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)

    def clean(self):
        if self.fields_dirty("status") and self.status == "closed" and not self.closed_at:
            raise ValidationError("Closing a ticket requires closed_at.")

fields_dirty(*names) is True if any of the named fields changed since the instance was loaded from the database. New instances always return True, so cross-field rules fire fully on create.

docs.title: Formsets and Editable Tables
docs.text: formwork_modelformset_factory and formwork_inlineformset_factory build model formsets on top of Django's. They validate uniqueness with one query per check instead of one per row, and they render as an editable table. Every name on this page is importable from django_formwork.

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
from django_formwork import formwork_inlineformset_factory, formwork_modelformset_factory

TaskFormSet = formwork_modelformset_factory(Task, fields=["title", "status"], extra=0)
LineFormSet = formwork_inlineformset_factory(Invoice, InvoiceLine, fields=["description", "quantity"])

Both take the arguments of Django's modelformset_factory and inlineformset_factory. Three defaults differ:

Argument Default form FormworkModelForm formset FormworkBaseModelFormSet / FormworkBaseInlineFormSet renderer FormworkRenderer()

To add formset behavior, subclass the base class and pass it as formset:

from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError

from django_formwork import FormworkBaseModelFormSet, formwork_modelformset_factory


class TaskBaseFormSet(FormworkBaseModelFormSet):
    def clean(self):
        super().clean()
        if sum(form.cleaned_data.get("hours", 0) for form in self.forms) > 40:
            raise ValidationError("More than 40 hours in one week.")


TaskFormSet = formwork_modelformset_factory(Task, formset=TaskBaseFormSet, fields=["title", "hours"])

docs.title: Uniqueness validation
docs.text:
Django validates uniqueness one form at a time: each row runs one query per unique check, so 50 rows with 3 checks make 150 queries. A Formwork formset takes these checks from its forms and runs one query per distinct check for all rows. The errors, their messages and their placement (on the field or in __all__) are the same as Django's. Only the query count changes.

One query covers all rows for:

  • unique, unique_together and unique_for_date / unique_for_month / unique_for_year.
  • A UniqueConstraint on fields only, with no condition, the default violation_error_message and nulls_distinct not set to False.
  • Every CheckConstraint.

These still run per row, through Django's own constraint.validate():

  • A UniqueConstraint with a condition, expressions, a custom message or nulls_distinct=False.
  • A UniqueConstraint over a GeneratedField or a field with a db_collation.

The database checks run in the formset's full_clean(), before validate_max and clean(), as Django runs them in each form's full_clean(). A clean() override without super() skips only the check between the submitted rows, as in Django. Rows marked for deletion are checked too, and the formset drops their errors, as Django does.

A plain ModelForm passed as form keeps Django's per-form checks.

docs.title: Known differences
docs.text:
Two cases compare values in Python where Django compares them in SQL:

  • A unique or unique_together field with a case-insensitive collation (MySQL *_ci, db_collation="NOCASE", PostgreSQL citext). The batched check can miss a duplicate that differs only in case. The database then rejects the save with an IntegrityError.
  • unique_for_date (or month, year) against a DateTimeField with a TIME_ZONE other than UTC. The batched check keys rows by the stored UTC date, Django by the local date, so a row near midnight can miss its duplicate.

docs.title: Editable tables
docs.text:
formset.as_rows(save_url) renders the formset as one <table>, with a header row from the formset's empty_form. form.as_row(save_url) renders one FormworkForm or FormworkModelForm as a <tbody>, with one cell per visible field and the hidden inputs in the first cell.

With a save_url, each row posts its own fields to that URL 400 ms after a change and morphs the response in place. Without one, the rows are static.

A disabled field shows as text: the instance's get_<field>_display(), else the instance's value (a comma-separated list for a many-to-many field), else the labels of the chosen values.

as_rows() does not render the management form. Add {{ formset.management_form }} if the table is also submitted as a whole formset.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Template Renders Set per class on formwork/tables/table.html as_rows(): the <table> the formset, template_name_table formwork/tables/row.html as_row(): one <tbody> the form, template_name_row

To override one for the whole project, put a template at the same path in a directory of your TEMPLATES setting.

docs.title: Saving a row
docs.text:
FormworkRowSaveMixin is the view behind save_url. It saves the posted row and answers with the row rendered again.

# views.py
from django.shortcuts import render
from django.urls import reverse
from django.views import View

from django_formwork import FormworkRowSaveMixin


class TaskRowSave(FormworkRowSaveMixin, View):
    form_class = TaskRowForm
    http_method_names = ["post"]

    def get_queryset(self, request):
        return Task.objects.filter(owner=request.user)


def task_list(request):
    formset = TaskFormSet(queryset=Task.objects.filter(owner=request.user))
    return render(request, "tasks/list.html", {"table": formset.as_rows(reverse("task_row_save"))})

# urls.py
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required

urlpatterns = [
    path("tasks/row/", login_required(TaskRowSave.as_view()), name="task_row_save"),
]

On each post the view:

  1. Reads the form prefix and the row's primary key from the post.
  2. Looks the row up in get_queryset(request). A missing or malformed key, or a row outside the queryset, gets a 404.
  3. Binds form_class(request.POST, request.FILES, instance=row, prefix=prefix).
  4. Saves the form if it is valid, and answers with the row, errors included.

queryset or get_queryset() is required. It holds the rows a user can change, so a user cannot post another user's primary key and edit that row. Without either, the view raises ImproperlyConfigured. Set queryset = Task.objects.all() only if every user can change every row. The mixin does no other access check: protect the view as you protect any other.

Method Default get_queryset(request) queryset.all() get_form_kwargs() {}, extra arguments for form_class get_prefix(request) the posted _formwork_prefix get_save_url(request) request.path render_row(request, form) form.as_row(self.get_save_url(request))

The form validates every field of form_class against the post: a required field the row does not post fails, and an optional one can be saved empty. Give the row form only the columns the table shows.

docs.title: Hand-authored rows
docs.text: To lay a row out yourself, render it from your own template and override render_row() to render the same template. Put {{ form.row_hidden_inputs }} in the row: it carries the prefix and the primary key the view reads. The full example renders its task list this way.

docs.title: FORMWORK_FORCE_ASYNC
docs.text:
Django's formsets have no async API: they validate and save their forms through the sync methods. The forms that a Formwork formset builds are therefore exempt from FORMWORK_FORCE_ASYNC. In an async view, run the formset's methods in a worker thread:

from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async

if await sync_to_async(formset.is_valid)():
    await sync_to_async(formset.save)()

Because these forms validate through the sync path, an async clean_<field>() or clean() on them is not awaited. Keep those methods sync on a formset's form.

A Django formset (modelformset_factory) with a FormworkModelForm gets no exemption: with the setting on, its is_valid() raises RuntimeError. Build it with formwork_modelformset_factory instead.

docs.title: Server-side Views
docs.text: Formwork has two views: FormworkSearchView serves the server-side search of every dropdown, and FormworkValidateView is the base class for a textarea validation endpoint. Both are importable from django_formwork (or from django_formwork.views).

docs.title: Server-side search
docs.text: Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox and ComboBoxMultiple search on the server when the widget gets a search_queryset. You configure the search on the widget; you write no URL and no view.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
# urls.py
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path("__formwork__/", include("django_formwork.urls")),
]

This mounts one URL, __formwork__/search/<key>/ (name formwork:search), which FormworkSearchView serves for every registered search.

docs.title: Configure a widget
docs.text:
# forms.py
from django import forms
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required

from django_formwork import FormworkForm, widgets

from .models import City


def cities(request):
    return City.objects.filter(active=True).select_related("country")


class CityForm(FormworkForm):
    city = forms.ModelChoiceField(
        queryset=City.objects.filter(active=True),
        widget=widgets.Select(
            search_queryset=cities,
            search_fields=["name", "country__name"],
            search_decorator=login_required,
        ),
    )
Parameter Description search_queryset callable(request, **params) that returns the rows to search. The endpoint calls it for each request, so it can scope the rows to the user. search_fields Field paths that the query matches with __icontains (or ranks, with search_ranked). Without them the endpoint does not filter: search_queryset reads request.GET["q"] itself and returns its rows best first. search_decorator Required. A view decorator that wraps the endpoint, such as login_required or permission_required("app.view_city"). Pass None for a public endpoint. search_ranked Orders the rows by match quality on PostgreSQL. See Ranked search. search_key, search_params Reuse another field's search with its own params. See Search templates. allow_clear Select and SelectMultiple: the list starts with the empty choice of an optional field (empty_label of a ModelChoiceField), so the user can clear it.

The form class registers each search when Python creates it, under a stable key built from the module, the form class, the field name, and the place where search_queryset and search_decorator are defined, so forms that a factory builds over one model keep their own search. Formwork imports the forms module of every installed app at startup, so a search declared there exists in every worker before the first request. A form defined elsewhere registers when its module is first imported. Registration raises ImproperlyConfigured for a widget without search_decorator, for a search_queryset that is not callable, for search_fields without search_queryset, and for search_ranked without search_fields or outside PostgreSQL.

search_queryset filters through the request it gets, never through values it closes over. The endpoint serves one search per key, so a second form of the same name whose search_queryset closes over other values raises ImproperlyConfigured.

The endpoint renders each row with label_from_instance of the field, so a ChoiceLabel adds an icon, a description or a trigger class to the results. A ComboBox over a CharField takes its own label_from_instance= and falls back to str().

docs.title: Paging
docs.text:
The widget renders the first 20 rows itself, plus the selected rows that lie past them. A search returns the next 20 matches at most. When more exist, the list ends with a hint and a "Load more" button that fetches the next page. The endpoint fetches one row past the page to tell whether more exist, so it never runs a COUNT. The first "Load more" request excludes the selected rows that the widget already shows past the first page.

With static choices and no search_queryset, the widget filters in the browser. It shows the search box past search_threshold (10) options, or when show_search=True.

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
search_decorator wraps FormworkSearchView.dispatch for that search. Every search needs an explicit value, and a widget without one raises ImproperlyConfigured when its form class registers:

from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required, permission_required

widgets.Select(search_queryset=cities, search_fields=["name"], search_decorator=login_required)
widgets.Select(
    search_queryset=cities,
    search_fields=["name"],
    search_decorator=permission_required("geo.view_city"),
)
widgets.Select(search_queryset=cities, search_fields=["name"], search_decorator=None)  # public

A request for an unknown key from an anonymous user redirects to settings.LOGIN_URL when django.contrib.auth is installed, so the response does not tell a missing key from a protected one. Otherwise an unknown key returns 404. Queries longer than FormworkSearchView.MAX_QUERY_LENGTH (200) characters are truncated.

FormworkSearchView is final: configure a search through the widget, not by subclassing the view.

docs.title: Ranked search
docs.text:
search_ranked=True orders the rows by how well they match, and matches typos too. It needs PostgreSQL with the pg_trgm extension, and at least one search_fields entry.

widgets.Select(
    search_queryset=cities,
    search_fields=["name"],
    search_ranked=True,
    search_decorator=login_required,
)

Rows that contain the query come first, then typo matches. Within each group, whole-word matches rank above partial ones, and the closest value comes first. A query shorter than 3 characters has too few trigrams to rank by, so it ranks exact matches first, then prefix matches, then the other rows that contain the query.

A GIN trigram index on UPPER(field::text) per search field serves every lookup of the ranked search and of plain __icontains:

from django.contrib.postgres.indexes import GinIndex, OpClass
from django.db import models
from django.db.models import TextField
from django.db.models.functions import Cast, Upper


class City(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            GinIndex(
                OpClass(Upper(Cast("name", output_field=TextField())), name="gin_trgm_ops"),
                name="city_name_trgm",
            ),
        ]

Create the extension in a migration with django.contrib.postgres.operations.TrigramExtension(). Without search_ranked, __icontains runs as LIKE '%query%'; the leading wildcard rules out a B-tree index, so a large table needs the same trigram index.

ranked_search(queryset, fields, query) in django_formwork.search applies the same ordering to any queryset.

docs.title: Search templates
docs.text:
A form that builds fields in __init__ (one field per group, for example) reuses one registered search with its own params. Declare a template field whose search_queryset takes keyword-only int or str params after the request, then pass its search_key and the params to the fields you build:

from django import forms
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

from django_formwork import FormworkForm, widgets


def group_members(request, *, group: int):
    return User.objects.filter(groups=group)


class TeamForm(FormworkForm):
    members_template = forms.ModelMultipleChoiceField(
        queryset=User.objects.none(),
        widget=widgets.SelectMultiple(
            search_queryset=group_members,
            search_fields=["email"],
            search_decorator=login_required,
        ),
    )

    def __init__(self, *args, groups, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        key = self.fields.pop("members_template").widget.search_key
        for group in groups:
            self.fields[f"group_{group.pk}"] = forms.ModelMultipleChoiceField(
                queryset=User.objects.filter(groups=group),
                widget=widgets.SelectMultiple(search_key=key, search_params={"group": group.pk}),
            )

The params travel in the search URL, and the endpoint converts them to the declared type before it calls search_queryset. The widget raises ImproperlyConfigured when the params do not match the declared names, and a param cannot take a name the endpoint reads itself (q, offset, exclude, widget, allow_clear). A user can edit the params in the URL, so search_queryset must return only rows that the requesting user is allowed to see, whatever the params say.

docs.title: FormworkValidateView
docs.text:
Base view for server-side textarea validation. It answers a POST, calls get_errors(text, request=request), and returns two fragments:

  1. The text as HTML, with <mark> tags around the error spans. htmx swaps it into the highlight overlay of the ValidatedTextarea.
  2. An out-of-band (hx-swap-oob) fragment with the error messages. htmx swaps it into the error area of the widget.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# views.py
import re

from django_formwork import FormworkValidateView

TYPOS = {"teh": "the", "recieve": "receive"}


class SpellCheckView(FormworkValidateView):
    def get_errors(self, text: str, **kwargs) -> list[dict]:
        return [
            {
                "message": f"Did you mean {TYPOS[word.group().lower()]!r}?",
                "start": word.start(),
                "end": word.end(),
            }
            for word in re.finditer(r"\w+", text)
            if word.group().lower() in TYPOS
        ]

# urls.py
from django.urls import path

from .views import SpellCheckView

urlpatterns = [
    path("validate/spell/", SpellCheckView.as_view(), name="spell-check"),
]

# forms.py
from django import forms
from django.urls import reverse_lazy

from django_formwork.widgets import ValidatedTextarea


class PostForm(forms.Form):
    content = forms.CharField(
        widget=ValidatedTextarea(validate_url=reverse_lazy("spell-check")),
    )

The widget posts only when the textarea has an id; see ValidatedTextarea.

docs.title: Error dict keys
docs.text:
Key Required Description message Yes Error description displayed below the textarea start No Start character index in the text (for highlight) end No End character index in the text (for highlight)

When an error has both start and end, the overlay wraps the text between those indices in a <mark> tag. The view merges overlapping spans into one <mark> and drops a span that lies outside the text.

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
Like the search side's search_decorator, the view exposes a validate_decorator hook. Set it on your subclass to wrap dispatch with a standard Django auth decorator:

from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required


class SpellCheckView(FormworkValidateView):
    validate_decorator = login_required

None (the default) leaves the endpoint public. Set a decorator on a subclass that does expensive work, such as a spell check, an LLM call or a database lookup: without one, anyone can call the endpoint, and formwork applies no rate limit.

docs.title: MAX_TEXT_LENGTH
docs.text: The view truncates the text to MAX_TEXT_LENGTH characters (default 50_000) before it calls get_errors(), as MAX_QUERY_LENGTH does on the search side. Override the class attribute to change the limit.

docs.title: Security note
docs.text:
FormworkValidateView is CSRF-exempt, because it only reads the posted text and returns the highlighted output. It changes no application state.

Read-only checks only

Subclass FormworkValidateView only for a read-only check. An operation that writes to the database, sends an email or changes other state needs a regular Django view with CSRF protection.

docs.title: Widget Reference
docs.text:
All widgets are in django_formwork.widgets. Their names follow Django's and shadow django.forms on purpose, so import the module:

from django import forms

from django_formwork import widgets

country = forms.ChoiceField(choices=[("de", "Germany"), ("fr", "France")], widget=widgets.Select)

TextInput, Textarea, PasswordInput, DateInput, CheckboxInput, CheckboxSelectMultiple, Select, SelectMultiple and ClearableFileInput are drop-ins for the Django widgets of the same name: validation is unchanged. Formwork never overrides a built-in widget template, so Django's own widgets keep their markup and get their DaisyUI look from formwork.css.

DaisyUI component-layer classes (alert, btn, loading, dropdown-content) appear directly in widget templates. Only the utility-layer DaisyUI classes (.input, .select) are applied via @apply in formwork.css, because they live in @layer utilities and would otherwise beat user component-layer overrides.

docs.title: Color variants
docs.text:
Every form-control widget accepts DaisyUI color modifiers through its class attr. This works the same on the widgets that are not real <select> elements (Select and SelectMultiple render a <details>/<summary>, ComboBox renders a text <input>). The modifiers are safelisted in formwork.css, so they compile even though the class is injected at render time and never appears in a template that Tailwind scans.

The color class is keyed to the underlying DaisyUI base, not the widget name:

Base Widgets Example class select-* Select, SelectMultiple, native <select> select-accent, select-soft input-* ComboBox, TextInput, DataList, native text inputs input-accent, input-soft textarea-* Textarea, ValidatedTextarea, native <textarea> textarea-accent, textarea-soft

ComboBox is an .input, so it takes input-accent / input-soft, not the select- prefix, even though it behaves like a select.

docs.title: Border color (DaisyUI built-in)
docs.text:
The eight DaisyUI colors tint the control's border:

city = forms.ChoiceField(
    widget=widgets.Select(attrs={"class": "select-accent"}),
    choices=CITIES,
)

docs.title: Soft fill (-soft)
docs.text:
formwork.css adds a -soft variant (DaisyUI ships none for form controls) that colors the whole control: a light tinted background with colored text, mirroring DaisyUI's btn-soft / alert-soft look. It composes with the color modifiers:

widgets.Select(attrs={"class": "select-soft select-accent"})
widgets.ComboBox(attrs={"class": "input-soft input-accent"})

-soft also follows the validation state: an aria-invalid control (or an explicit select-error) renders a red-tinted fill, because both the error state and -soft flow through the same --input-color variable. Used on its own (no color modifier), -soft gives a readable neutral fill.

docs.title: Floating labels
docs.text:
Widgets: TextInput, Textarea, PasswordInput, Select, SelectMultiple

Pass floating=True to reuse a control's placeholder as a DaisyUI floating label: the placeholder text sits inside the control when empty and floats above it on focus or fill. The widget wraps the control in <label class="floating-label"> with a <span> that carries the label text, and that wrapper becomes the accessible name, so CSS hides the redundant field legend. A floating widget without a placeholder raises ImproperlyConfigured.

nickname = forms.CharField(
    widget=widgets.TextInput(attrs={"placeholder": "Nickname"}, floating=True),
)
note = forms.CharField(
    widget=widgets.Textarea(attrs={"placeholder": "Note"}, floating=True),
)
role = forms.ChoiceField(
    choices=[("", ""), ("admin", "Admin"), ("user", "User")],
    widget=widgets.Select(attrs={"placeholder": "Role"}, floating=True),
)

On a select, the label always floats above the trigger.

docs.title: ChoiceLabel
docs.text:
ChoiceLabel is a choice label whose str() is its text. The extras are presentation only, so validation and cleaned_data see a plain label. It is importable from django_formwork and from django_formwork.widgets.

Parameter Type Default Description label str The option text icon str "" HTML before the text; mark it safe description str "" A second line under the text label_html str "" HTML that replaces the text in the row and the trigger; mark it safe color BadgeColor "neutral" Badge color in Display(badges=True): one of the eight DaisyUI colors selected_toggle_class str "" Classes that Select puts on its closed trigger while this option is selected

Use it in choices, or return it from label_from_instance for a model field:

from django.utils.html import format_html

from django_formwork import ChoiceLabel


priority = forms.ChoiceField(
    choices=[
        ("low", ChoiceLabel("Low", selected_toggle_class="select-success")),
        ("mid", ChoiceLabel("Medium", selected_toggle_class="select-warning")),
        ("high", ChoiceLabel("High", selected_toggle_class="select-error")),
    ],
    widget=widgets.Select,
)


class MemberChoiceField(forms.ModelChoiceField):
    def label_from_instance(self, obj):
        return ChoiceLabel(
            obj.name,
            icon=format_html('<span class="badge badge-ghost badge-sm">{}</span>', obj.initials),
            description=obj.email,
        )

selected_toggle_class applies on the first render, after a validation error, and on every pick in the browser, with no round-trip. Formwork passes the string through unchanged, so any class works.

The class only styles the trigger if it exists in your compiled CSS. formwork.css safelists every {select,input,textarea}-{color} and badge-{color} class. A literal class name in a template or a Python file that Tailwind scans compiles too. A class name that your code builds at render time (f"select-{level}") needs an @source inline("...") line in your Tailwind entry point.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.Select

Single-select dropdown: a <details>/<summary> trigger with a popover panel. A hidden input posts the value, so the submitted value is a key from the choices. The panel is at most 288px tall and scrolls. The trigger shows DaisyUI's caret, the selected option's icon, and "Select…" while nothing is selected. A disabled field greys the trigger out.

A search box appears past search_threshold (10) options and filters the list in the browser. With a search_queryset, the widget searches on the server instead; see Server-side search.

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes; class goes on the trigger choices iterable () Choices, as for forms.Select show_search bool \| None None True or False forces the search box; None shows it past the threshold or when the list is truncated show_spinner bool True Spinner in the search box during a server search allow_clear bool False Offer the empty choice as a row that clears the value floating bool False Floating label search_queryset callable \| None None callable(request, **params) that returns the rows to search search_fields Sequence[str] \| None None Field paths the query matches search_decorator callable \| None required with search_queryset Access rule for the search; None for a public endpoint search_ranked bool False Rank the results on PostgreSQL search_key, search_params None Reuse a registered search with its own params counts Mapping \| None None A number at the end of each option, keyed by the option value, as faceted filters show; a value missing from the mapping shows 0, dimmed. A list that the server pages shows no counts 
city = forms.ChoiceField(choices=CITIES, widget=widgets.Select)

assignee = MemberChoiceField(
    queryset=Member.objects.all(),
    required=False,
    empty_label="Unassigned",
    widget=widgets.Select(
        search_queryset=lambda request: Member.objects.all(),
        search_fields=["name", "email"],
        search_decorator=login_required,
        allow_clear=True,
    ),
)

Option groups render as headings. For a domain choice set, such as a country select with flag icons, subclass Select in your project and set the choices; formwork ships no domain widgets.

docs.title: SelectMultiple
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.SelectMultiple

Multi-select dropdown with a checkbox per option. It takes every parameter of Select, plus open_icon. The closed trigger lists the selected labels with their icons. Past summary_threshold (3) selections it shows a count ("4 selected") instead. With a server search, hidden inputs post the selected values, because the list holds only one page.

Parameter Type Default Description open_icon str \| None None A Lucide icon name that replaces DaisyUI's caret on the trigger 
languages = forms.MultipleChoiceField(
    choices=[("py", "Python"), ("js", "JavaScript")],
    widget=widgets.SelectMultiple,
)

tags = forms.ModelMultipleChoiceField(
    queryset=Tag.objects.all(),
    required=False,
    widget=widgets.SelectMultiple(
        search_queryset=lambda request: Tag.objects.all(),
        search_fields=["name"],
        search_decorator=login_required,
    ),
)

docs.title: ComboBox
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.TextInput

Text input with a suggestion dropdown. The submitted value is whatever the user typed; the suggestions are hints.

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes for the <input> suggestions sequence None Strings or ChoiceLabels, flat or grouped as [(group, [...])] show_spinner bool True Spinner during a server search search_queryset, search_fields, search_decorator, search_ranked, search_key, search_params As on Select; the search fills the list on first focus and on typing label_from_instance callable \| None None Turns a searched row into the suggestion label when the field has no label_from_instance of its own, as on a CharField; str() otherwise 
food = forms.CharField(
    widget=widgets.ComboBox(
        suggestions=[
            ChoiceLabel("Pizza", icon=PIZZA_ICON),
            "Pasta",
            ("Asian", ["Sushi", "Ramen", "Curry"]),
        ],
    ),
)

A picked suggestion's icon shows beside the text in the closed input.

docs.title: ComboBoxMultiple
docs.text:
Parent class: ComboBox

ComboBox for comma-separated free text. The suggestions apply to the segment that the user types.

tags = forms.CharField(widget=widgets.ComboBoxMultiple(suggestions=["pizza", "pasta", "sushi"]))

docs.title: TextInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.TextInput

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes floating bool False Floating label input_type str "text" The text-like type: email, tel, url, and so on

TextInput mixes in PatternHintMixin.

docs.title: Textarea
docs.text: Parent class: forms.Textarea. Takes attrs and floating.

docs.title: PasswordInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.PasswordInput

Password input with a button that shows the typed text.

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes render_value bool False As on forms.PasswordInput floating bool False Floating label reveal bool True False drops the show button

docs.title: SearchInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.TextInput, with input_type = "search"

Search field with a leading magnifier, an htmx spinner while a request runs, and a clear button. The default placeholder is "Search...".

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes show_spinner bool True Swap the magnifier for a spinner during an htmx request show_clear bool True Show the clear button filter_items str "" CSS selector: typing hides the matching rows whose data-label misses the query 
q = forms.CharField(
    required=False,
    widget=widgets.SearchInput(filter_items="#task-list [data-label]"),
)

docs.title: DataList
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.TextInput

Text input with native <datalist> suggestions. The browser draws the list, so it needs no JavaScript. The submitted value is free text.

browser = forms.CharField(widget=widgets.DataList(suggestions=["Chrome", "Firefox", "Safari"]))

docs.title: InputMask
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.TextInput

Text input with a fixed-format mask that Alpine enforces as the user types. Mask tokens: # is a digit, A a letter, * any character. The placeholder shows the mask.

phone = forms.CharField(widget=widgets.InputMask(mask="(###) ###-####"))

docs.title: OTPInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.TextInput

One-time code of length digits (default 6) in a single input, drawn as one box per digit. One real input keeps SMS autofill and paste working. It sets inputmode="numeric", autocomplete="one-time-code", maxlength and a pattern, and needs no JavaScript.

code = forms.CharField(widget=widgets.OTPInput(length=6))

docs.title: ValidatedTextarea
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.Textarea

Textarea with server-side validation and highlighting. With validate_url, htmx posts the text after a 500 ms pause in typing. The server returns highlighted HTML (with <mark> tags around errors) that overlays the textarea, plus the messages through an out-of-band swap. Without validate_url, it renders a plain textarea.

The live validation needs an id on the textarea, because the htmx target and the error area are built from it. A form field gets the id from the form's auto_id. With auto_id=False, or when you render the widget yourself without attrs={"id": ...}, the textarea sends no validation request.

content = forms.CharField(
    widget=widgets.ValidatedTextarea(validate_url=reverse_lazy("spell-check")),
)

See FormworkValidateView for the server side. The live errors render in the widget's own tooltip, whatever the form's error_display. A field-level error such as required still renders where error_display puts it, so the two can show at the same time.

docs.title: StepperNumberInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.NumberInput

Number input between a - and a + button that step it by its step attribute. The value is clamped when the user commits it.

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes, such as step and max integer bool False Drop the decimals min float \| None None Lower bound for the buttons, without a native min attribute trailing_buttons bool False Put both buttons after the input 
seats = forms.IntegerField(widget=widgets.StepperNumberInput(integer=True, min=1))

docs.title: SuffixNumberInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.NumberInput

Number input with a static unit, currency or percent sign inside the field.

weight = forms.DecimalField(widget=widgets.SuffixNumberInput(suffix="kg"))
price = forms.DecimalField(widget=widgets.SuffixNumberInput(prefix="€"))

docs.title: Range
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.NumberInput, with input_type = "range"

volume = forms.IntegerField(widget=widgets.Range(attrs={"min": 0, "max": 100, "step": 5}))

docs.title: DateInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.DateInput

Native date input. Django's own widget renders type="text" with a locale format; the native control accepts only ISO, so format defaults to "%Y-%m-%d".

docs.title: DateRangePicker and DateRangeField
docs.text:
DateRangePicker shows a start and an end date as two text inputs in one box. A click or the focus opens a calendar with two months side by side, one on a phone. The first click on a day sets the start, the second the end, and the days in between fill in while the pointer moves. A click before the start begins the range again there. A click into the end input opens the calendar to change the end alone. The footer counts the days and has a Clear button.

The inputs also take typed dates. A date an input can read moves the calendar to its month and marks it, and Tab goes on from the start to the end. An input reads the format it shows, the formats in DATE_INPUT_FORMATS and ISO. Month names can be full or short, in any case, with or without the dot, so nov 8 2026 reads as November 8, 2026. When the focus leaves an input, a date it read shows in the display format. Text that names no date posts as typed: the field reports it and the input keeps the text. An end typed before the start is not swapped, and the field reports the order.

Use it through DateRangeField, which cleans to a DateRange(start, end) and uses the picker by default:

from datetime import timedelta

from django_formwork import DateRangeField

period = DateRangeField(
    max_span=timedelta(days=90),
    error_messages={"max_span": "Pick at most 90 days."},
)

required demands both dates. The field rejects a start after the end (start_after_end) and, with max_span, a range longer than that (max_span).

The widget posts each date as ISO in a hidden input (period_0, period_1). format sets how the inputs show them: a Django format setting name or a format string, DATE_FORMAT by default. Month and weekday names follow the active language, and the week starts on FIRST_DAY_OF_WEEK. Each input is as wide as the longest date the format writes, so the end keeps its place whatever the start holds. A short format fits a narrow column:

period = DateRangeField(widget=widgets.DateRangePicker(format="SHORT_DATE_FORMAT"))

presets=True adds four buttons under the calendar: Today, Past 7 days, This month and This year. A preset picks its whole range and closes the calendar. The days count in the current time zone, as in Django's admin date filter, and Past 7 days is today and the six days before it. For other ranges, pass a function that takes today and returns (label, start, end) tuples. DateRangePicker.default_presets returns the four above:

from datetime import timedelta

from django.utils.translation import gettext as _


def presets(today):
    past_30_days = (_("Past 30 days"), today - timedelta(days=29), today)
    return [*widgets.DateRangePicker.default_presets(today), past_30_days]


period = DateRangeField(widget=widgets.DateRangePicker(presets=presets))

The field label names the two inputs as a group. data-* and hx-* attrs go on the end's hidden input, which fires one change when the range changes. aria-describedby, aria-invalid and aria-required go on both text inputs, and the other attrs on the start input.

docs.title: DateTimeRangePicker and DateTimeRangeField
docs.text:
DateTimeRangeField cleans to a DateTimeRange(start, end) of two datetimes and uses DateTimeRangePicker. The calendar works as above, with a start time and an end time under it and a Done button that closes it. The times start at 00:00 and 23:59. The inputs post YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM in the current time zone, and an aware value shows in it.

A typed date can carry a time, in the display format or in a format from DATETIME_INPUT_FORMATS: 3/1/2030 14:30 or Mar. 1, 2030, 2:30 p.m.. A date typed without a time takes the time under the calendar. A preset picks its days from 00:00 to 23:59.

from django_formwork import DateTimeRangeField

stay = DateTimeRangeField(max_span=timedelta(days=14))

format defaults to DATETIME_FORMAT.

docs.title: Two native date inputs
docs.text:
DateRangeField also takes Django's own MultiWidget. With two DateInputs it shows the browser's date controls side by side under one field label. The label names the pair, so give each input an aria-label:

from django import forms
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _
from django_formwork import DateRangeField, widgets

period = DateRangeField(
    widget=forms.MultiWidget(
        [
            widgets.DateInput(attrs={"aria-label": _("From")}),
            widgets.DateInput(attrs={"aria-label": _("To")}),
        ]
    ),
)

The inputs post period_0 and period_1, like DateRangePicker.

docs.title: DatePicker
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.DateInput

Text date input with an Alpine calendar dropdown, for a page where the native DateInput does not fit. format sets how the input shows the date, both when the server renders it and after a pick in the calendar, and the placeholder shows that format. The widget reads the format back, and also YYYY-MM-DD, so the field needs no matching input_formats.

due_date = forms.DateField(widget=widgets.DatePicker)
delivery = forms.DateField(widget=widgets.DatePicker(format="%d.%m.%Y"))

A click on the month title switches to a month grid, and a click on the year to a year grid. The arrow keys move a day or a week, Page Up and Page Down a month, with Shift a year. The calendar follows the active language and FIRST_DAY_OF_WEEK, like the range pickers, and has Today and Clear buttons.

Month and weekday names (%B, %b, %A, %a) are the English ones that Python's strftime writes.

docs.title: CheckboxInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.CheckboxInput

Without text, the field label sits beside the box. With text, the field label sits above the box and text beside it:

terms = forms.BooleanField(
    label="Terms",
    widget=widgets.CheckboxInput(text="I accept the terms of service"),
)

docs.title: ToggleInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.CheckboxInput

Checkbox drawn as a DaisyUI toggle switch, with the field label beside it and no background. The label turns full strength while the switch is on.

dark_mode = forms.BooleanField(widget=widgets.ToggleInput(attrs={"class": "toggle-primary"}), required=False)

docs.title: CheckboxSelectMultiple
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple

Drop-in for Django's widget. Checkbox and radio groups render as plain stacked rows with no background box. Pass columns=2 for a two-column grid.

docs.title: CardRadioSelect and CardCheckboxSelectMultiple
docs.text:
Parent classes: forms.RadioSelect, forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple

Choices drawn as large selectable cards with the label text centered, stacked on small screens and side by side from the lg breakpoint. The checked card fills with the primary color.

plan = forms.ChoiceField(
    choices=[("free", "Free"), ("pro", "Pro")],
    widget=widgets.CardRadioSelect,
)

docs.title: Rating
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.RadioSelect

Star rating with DaisyUI's rating component.

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes for the radio inputs star_class str "mask-star-2" DaisyUI mask class for the star shape allow_clear bool False Add a hidden first radio that clears the rating

Rating.make_choices(max_stars=5) returns [("1", "1 star"), ("2", "2 stars"), ...]. Use it instead of writing the choices yourself; choices is a reserved property name on ChoiceWidget.

rating = forms.TypedChoiceField(
    choices=widgets.Rating.make_choices(5),
    coerce=int,
    widget=widgets.Rating(star_class="mask-heart", allow_clear=True),
)

docs.title: Files
docs.text: Django's own ClearableFileInput works without changes: formwork.css puts the stored file and the clear box on one line and the file input under them.

docs.title: ClearableFileInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.ClearableFileInput

A file upload in one row, as high as a text input. The row shows the stored file as a link, with an icon for its type, and a click anywhere on it opens the file picker.

delivery_note = forms.FileField(required=False, widget=widgets.ClearableFileInput)
Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes; {"multiple": True} picks several files and needs MultipleFileField max_size int \| None None Largest file in bytes, checked in the browser

On an optional field, the × button checks Django's clear box, and the field cleans to False. Until the save, the name is struck through and a second button keeps the file. A file picked after the clear unchecks the box again, so Django gets the new file and no "submit a file or check the clear checkbox" error. A required field has no clear box, as in Django's widget.

The icon follows the extension. PDF files, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, images, archives, audio, video and code each have their own icon, and other files get a plain file icon. FileDropzoneInput uses the same icons.

docs.title: FileDropzoneInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.FileInput

Dashed drop area that takes dragged files or opens the file picker. max_size (bytes) rejects larger files in the browser.

docs = forms.FileField(
    widget=widgets.FileDropzoneInput(attrs={"accept": ".pdf"}, max_size=10 * 1024 * 1024),
)

For several files, use MultipleFileField. Its default widget is this drop area with multiple, and it cleans to a list of files. A plain FileField rejects the list that a multiple input sends.

from django_formwork import MultipleFileField

attachments = MultipleFileField(required=False)

required demands at least one file, and each file gets the FileField checks, such as the one for an empty file. No model field holds several files, so save each one yourself, for example as a row of a related model. For other widget options, pass widget=widgets.FileDropzoneInput(attrs={"multiple": True, ...}).

docs.title: ImageDropzoneInput
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.FileInput

Drop area that previews the stored image, with a button that clears it. accept defaults to image/*.

Parameter Type Default Description attrs dict \| None None HTML attributes, merged over {"accept": "image/*"} max_size int \| None None Largest file in bytes, checked in the browser hint str "" A line of text in the drop area preview_url str \| None None Replaces the stored file's URL; "" hides the preview

On an optional field, the clear button posts clear_<name>, and the field cleans to False, which clears the stored file, as with ClearableFileInput. After the clear, the drop area comes back, and a file picked there replaces the stored one.

Server-side validation

accept and max_size only guide the browser. Validate the file type and size on the server as well.

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
Parent class: forms.Widget

A value the user cannot change, in the box of a filled field. It posts nothing, so put it on a disabled field. Each item is a string or a ChoiceLabel; with badges=True, each item is a badge in its color.

status = forms.Field(
    disabled=True,
    required=False,
    widget=widgets.Display(badges=True),
)
form = OrderForm(initial={"status": [ChoiceLabel("Paid", color="success")]})

docs.title: PatternHintMixin
docs.text:
Shows the class attribute pattern_hint under a text control while its value misses the pattern attribute. CSS reads the browser's verdict, so it needs no JavaScript. Pair it with a server-side validator.

class PostcodeInput(widgets.TextInput):
    pattern_hint = _("Five digits, for example 10115")

    def __init__(self, attrs=None):
        super().__init__({"pattern": "[0-9]{5}", **(attrs or {})})

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Every widget with a Media class needs Alpine.js on the page: Select, SelectMultiple, ComboBox, DatePicker, DateRangePicker, DateTimeRangePicker, StepperNumberInput, PasswordInput, SearchInput, ClearableFileInput, FileDropzoneInput, ImageDropzoneInput, InputMask and ValidatedTextarea. A server search and ValidatedTextarea need htmx as well. The installation guide shows the script order.
